summary.title: The Problems with Deliberate Practice
summary.one_liner: Deliberate practice is hard to apply to careers, because its two core claims (talent matters little, and only deliberate practice builds mastery) are contested and most non-music, non-chess fields lack the established training methods it requires.
keywords: how to learn a skill deliberately
takeaways: Ericsson's 'deliberate practice' is distinct from Gladwell's popularised '10,000 hour rule', and the claim that talent is overrated is under academic criticism.
Deliberate practice requires well-established training methods, a teacher in early stages, and building on existing skills; these are hard to find in many careers.
Purposeful practice principles (focus, discomfort, feedback, specific goals) can be applied even where no standard training exists.
Self-learners face three main problems: ill-defined sub skills, lack of feedback, and lack of practice opportunities, plus loss of motivation from plateaus.
Workarounds include comparing your moves with an expert's, reproducing admired passages, spaced repetition with Anki, and recording yourself for review.
summary.summary: The author, a programmer who has tried to apply deliberate practice to writing, management and career skills, first reviews academic criticisms of Anders Ericsson's claims: inconsistent definitions, overly broad universality claims in the popular book Peak, weak effect sizes in meta-analyses, and few falsification attempts. He then turns to practical use, separating purposeful practice from the extra requirements of deliberate practice (established training methods, teacher guidance, building on prior skills). He argues that self-learners in fields without standard curricula must do their own skill extraction, syllabus design and feedback design, and suggests workarounds such as the chess and Franklin reproduction techniques, Anki, and self-recording.
